sections.h2: How Caldwell County taxes a house
sections.html:
Three local offices touch your bill. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) puts a value on the house, the Caldwell County Sheriff takes payment, and the clerk inherits whatever is still open once April 15 passes. Value is locked in on January 1, and the state expects the PVA to visit each parcel at least every four years.

Your total is a sum of several taxing districts, including the state, the county and the schools. Each one chooses its own rate, and the PVA plays no part in that choice.

This is farm country, where land in agricultural use is taxed for what it produces, not for what it would sell for. Ten or more acres kept for livestock or crops, timber included, can qualify. If you own acreage, find out from the PVA how your land is classed before you list it.

KRS 134.015 sets a monthly ladder that opens November 1 and closes April 15. Late October is when bills go out, now as letters instead of postcards. A payment counts for a phase if it is postmarked, handed over or dropped in the box before the next phase starts.

Inside the Princeton courthouse, look for the first door on the right off Main Street. Staff accept cash, checks, money orders and cashier's checks, plus cards at the counter for a surcharge. After hours, use the drop box by the east door, which cannot hold cash. The office keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 4 pm and publishes a holiday closing list each season.

sections.h2: Which office answers which tax question
sections.html:
Most questions end at one of three numbers: 270-365-2088 (sheriff), 270-365-7227 (PVA) and 270-365-6754 (clerk). The PVA works upstairs at 100 East Market Street, and mail for the sheriff goes to Room 25 in that building.

  • Sheriff: sends bills, takes payment through April 15, and offers an online search that only displays bills.
  • PVA: sets values, handles homestead and disability forms, and hosts the conference required before an appeal.
  • County clerk: inherits delinquent bills and records deeds.

Bills are addressed to the January 1 owner. The sheriff never receives deed transfers, so a new owner's name shows up in care-of form the first year. A buyer whose bill went to the seller can print it from the sheriff's site.

sections.h2: How to dispute a Caldwell County value
sections.html:
Your first move is a PVA conference. Next comes a filing at the clerk's office, due by the workday after public inspection ends. Inspection covers 13 days starting the first Monday in May, and the local appeals board meets for up to five days, starting 25 to 35 days after that.

The board wants paper, not opinions: lot and building descriptions, insurance documents, building costs, and listings of comparable sales. An appeal with none is denied. Going around the local board also forecloses any later review. Since bills may print while your case is pending, you are billed on your own claimed value, with a supplemental bill if the board rules higher.

The number that survives is the one a buyer's lender and title company will see. After a new roof or an addition, make sure the PVA's record matches the house today.

Owners who live in their home and are 65 or older, or totally disabled, get part of the assessed value taken off. The deduction was $46,350 for 2024 and 2025. KRS 132.810 resets it every two years, so ask the PVA for today's figure.

You must occupy the house you own, show proof of age and claim no exemption anywhere else. Filling out the form at the PVA office takes under five minutes. The benefit belongs to you, not the house, so your buyer files a new application.

Before closing, an older seller should look for the exemption on the bill. If it is absent, take it up with the PVA ahead of paying.

Owners who live away from Princeton, including heirs holding a house they plan to sell, have three workable routes. Mail a check to the sheriff at 100 East Market Street, Room 25, with the bill, and aim to post it before the end of the month so the postmark falls in the phase you want. Send someone to the courthouse counter. Or leave a check in the east-door drop box, which works at any hour except that it cannot hold cash.

The online search will show you the bill and its amount, though it will not take payment, and the sheriff does not take phone payments either. Print the bill and keep the receipt, because a title company may ask to see it.

sections.h2: What happens to the bill at closing
sections.html:
A tax lien stays on the parcel, and the closing agent divides the year between buyer and seller. Ask your agent or lender how the split was handled, because the sheriff is never told.

A sale does not erase an unpaid bill. Delinquent bills pass to the clerk along with penalties and 1% monthly interest, so back taxes call for a payoff figure from the clerk before you choose a closing date.

With escrow, the bill still comes to you, and passing it to the lender is your task. A periodic call to the servicer keeps a missed hand-off from turning into a penalty.

Princeton is the seat of a county of 12,609 residents, with 6,122 homes counted in mid-2025. A typical owner's home is valued at $118,500. Owners occupy 70.2% of homes, rent runs about $767 a month, and household income is typically $59,583.

Most residents stay put (93.4 percent were in the same home a year earlier), so the houses that do come up are often estates, older owners or farm families. An owner dealing with repairs or a tenant may prefer a direct cash sale in place of showings.

sections.h2: Steps before a Caldwell County sale
sections.html:
1. Phone the sheriff (270-365-2088) to learn if this year's bill is paid, and in which phase.
  2. Phone the clerk (270-365-6754) about any earlier year still open.
  3. Phone the PVA (270-365-7227) to check for a homestead exemption and, on acreage, the farmland classification.
  4. Pass each amount to the closing agent so it can be paid from your proceeds.

A cash buyer takes the house as-is, so repairs and showings drop away. Taxes do not: back taxes and liens come out of your proceeds either way. Starting these calls early leaves time to fix a wrong name or a missing exemption before a contract is signed.

faqs.q: What dates matter for Caldwell County tax bills?
faqs.a: Payment opens November 1, and the 2% discount holds through November 30. Face value applies in December, 5% is added in January, and 21% is added from February 1 to April 15. Whatever remains on April 15 moves to the county clerk.

faqs.q: Where can I pay a tax bill in Princeton?
faqs.a: Pay at the counter inside the courthouse, mail a check to 100 E. Market St., Room 25, or leave it in the east-door drop box. The online search displays bills only, and nobody takes payment by phone.

faqs.q: Is there a tax break for homeowners over 65 in Caldwell County?
faqs.a: Yes, the homestead exemption covers owners who live in the home and turn 65 during the year. Apply at the PVA office with proof of age. It trims the assessed value, and a new owner must apply again.

faqs.q: What if my Princeton house sells before the bill comes?
faqs.a: The bill is issued to the January 1 owner, so you may still get it. The closing agent prorates, and a buyer who never receives it can print a copy from the sheriff's site.

faqs.q: Do I need repairs before a cash sale in Caldwell County?
faqs.a: No. A cash buyer can take the house as-is. Back taxes and liens come out of your proceeds, so ask the sheriff and clerk for amounts early.
